title: Alcohol & Drugs
summary: How alcohol, medicines and other drugs affect your driving, what raises your BAC, how impaired-driving laws work, and how to always get home safely.

blocks.text: Alcohol is a depressant. It slows down your brain and body, even if you feel more energetic. Its effects start with the first drink, well before any legal limit.

rows: Affected first. Drinkers feel confident and decide they are fine to drive.
Slows down, so you need longer to respond to hazards.
Gets worse, including judging speed and distance. At night, it takes longer to recover from headlight glare.
Steering, braking and staying in your lane get harder.

blocks.text: Alcohol weakens your driving skills while making you feel more confident. That is why a drinker is a poor judge of whether they can drive. Years of driving experience do not protect you.
Young drivers who drink crash at lower blood alcohol levels than older, experienced drivers. Inexperience and alcohol are a dangerous mix.
Each of these holds about the same amount of alcohol. No type of drink is safer than another; what matters is how much alcohol you take in.
Large or specialty mixed drinks often contain more than one shot, so one glass can equal several standard drinks. Mixers do not reduce the alcohol.

sections.heading: What sets your BAC, and what does not lower it

blocks.text: Blood alcohol concentration (BAC) is the percentage of alcohol in your blood. It is measured with a breath, blood or urine test.

items: How much you drink: more drinks mean a higher BAC.
How fast you drink: three drinks in one hour raise your BAC more than three drinks over three hours.
Body weight: a lighter person reaches a higher BAC from the same amount.
Sex: a woman who drinks the same as a man of the same weight usually reaches a higher BAC.
Food: eating slows how fast alcohol is absorbed, but it cannot prevent impairment.

blocks.text: Only time lowers your BAC. Your liver breaks down most of the alcohol at a slow, steady rate, about one standard drink per hour on average. Some people take longer.

Coffee, cold showers, fresh air and exercise do not sober you up. Coffee may make you feel more alert, but your BAC stays the same. After heavy drinking, you can still be impaired the next morning, because sleep does not speed things up.

Impaired-driving laws cover any drug that affects your driving: illegal drugs, prescription medicines and over-the-counter products. A valid prescription, or marijuana that is legal where you live, does not make impaired driving legal.

rows: Some contain alcohol or ingredients that make you drowsy.
Can cause drowsiness and slow reactions, even at the normal dose.
Slows reactions and hurts judgment, coordination, attention, lane keeping and distance judgment.
May make you feel alert for a short time, but later can cause nervousness, dizziness, poor focus and vision problems. They are not a substitute for rest.

items: Read the label. "Do not operate heavy machinery" includes your car.
If you are not sure how a medicine will affect you, ask your doctor or pharmacist before you drive.
Never mix alcohol with other drugs. Their effects can multiply, so one beer plus an allergy pill can hit you like several drinks.
Every state sets a legal BAC limit for adult drivers, and lower limits for some groups. Check your state's numbers in your State Cheat Sheet.
Drivers under 21 face "zero tolerance" laws, with a limit far below the adult limit.
Being under the limit does not make it legal to drive impaired. If you are weaving or driving badly, an officer can arrest you based on what they see.
Implied consent: by driving in the state, you have already agreed to a breath, blood or urine test when an officer lawfully asks. Some states call this express consent.
Refusing the test carries its own penalties, such as losing your license, separate from any impaired-driving charge.
Chemical tests can detect other drugs, including medicines, not just alcohol.
A conviction for impaired driving can mean license suspension or revocation, fines, jail, required alcohol programs and an ignition interlock. Penalties vary by state; see your State Cheat Sheet.

blocks.text: Decide how you will get home before you start drinking. Once alcohol affects your judgment, you are less likely to make a safe choice.

items: A designated driver drinks no alcohol at all, not even one beer. "Drank the least" is not sober.
Other safe options: a taxi, rideshare, public transit, or staying the night.
If a friend has been drinking and wants to drive, take their keys and help them get a safe ride or a place to sleep.
If you host a party, serve food and alcohol-free drinks, do not push refills, and stop serving alcohol well before the party ends.
Weaving or drifting within or across lanes.
Jerky speed changes and braking for no reason.
Sudden stops at signs or lights.
Driving much faster, or much slower, than other traffic.

blocks.text: Stay well back from a driver who seems impaired. Have a passenger call police, or pull over safely to call, with the car's description, location and direction. Never try to stop the driver yourself.

keyPoints: Alcohol is a depressant that affects judgment first, so drinkers think they are fine to drive.
A 12-ounce beer, a glass of wine and a 1.5-ounce shot hold about the same alcohol; no drink is safer.
BAC depends on how much and how fast you drink, your weight, your sex and food; only time lowers it.
Coffee, cold showers and exercise do not sober you up, and sleep does not speed it up; the body clears about one drink per hour.
Prescription, over-the-counter and legal drugs can impair you, and mixing them with alcohol multiplies the effect.
Implied consent means you agreed to chemical testing; refusing has its own penalties. Under-21 drivers face zero tolerance. Check BAC limits in your State Cheat Sheet.
Plan a sober ride before drinking; a designated driver drinks nothing at all.
